Senses.Explanation: A comic epithet for a one-sided person: a fellow carrying a board and seeing only one side. The stock line says that Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side, while Baiyu Jingsi states directly that each party sees one side and is precisely a board-carrying fellow (各見一邊，正是擔板漢). In a case Baiyu raises, Muezhou Daozong calls to an addressee and applies the name when the man turns; Xuedou Chongxian and Huanglong Huinan then debate its application, and Baiyu judges their opposed comments one-sided. The label extends beyond that case. Dongshan Meixi Du says that learning without awakening is overbearing pride, whereas awakening without learning is a board-carrying fellow (有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢). Zhe'an Jingfan applies it both to delight at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket, and elsewhere says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients only makes such a fellow before asking how the matter can be raised whole (只成擔板漢，此事如何舉得全). Yuanwu Keqin says that a board-carrying fellow often dies in the phrase (若是擔板漢，多向句中死却). Zen bends a comic physical image into a public epithet for the person whom a record presents as fixed on one side or trapped in wording; the entry reports those attested applications without generalizing beyond them.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 193 times in 90 allowlisted texts; the shorter form for carrying a board (擔板) occurs 589 times in 186 texts. Six exact witnesses and one family witness cover the one-side formula, Muezhou case, paired formulas, and direct teaching-seat applications. These are local applications of one epithet, not separate referents.

SearchAliases: carry snow to fill a well
Senses.Explanation: Carrying snow to fill a well is a recurrent comparison for ineffective effort, applied to talk, question-and-answer, sitting Chan, and other undertakings. Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" : the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" , to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" , and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" . Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball . Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

The fixed appraisal ‘the substance stands exposed’ occurs in ‘true constancy stands exposed,’ ‘the whole substance stands exposed,’ and the recurrent ‘the substance stands exposed in the golden wind’ case; the grammar leaves ‘body’ versus ‘substance’ open where the record does. Literally, “body or substance” and “exposed”: “body or substance exposed.” The compound occurs 646 times in 222 allowlisted texts. Its syntax varies: the body or constant substance is exposed, while the preceding word “whole” can make the entire body exposed. One discourse explicitly says that when feelings about holy and ordinary are exhausted, this is called “true constancy, body exposed.” Another recurrent statement says, “True constancy, body exposed, not constrained by written words.” The fixed Yunmen exchange asks, “What about when the tree withers and the leaves fall?” and answers, “Body exposed in the autumn wind.” That four-graph answer occurs 176 times in 100 texts and is repeatedly raised, versified, and questioned by later masters. Other expansions include “body exposed, imposing and evident” and “the whole body exposed.”
Senses.Note: The entry does not choose an unstated referent for 'body' in every occurrence. It records the nouns and predicates supplied by each text. 'The whole body exposed' occurs 153 times in 95 texts, and 'fully exposed, imposing and evident' occurs 61 times in 49. The direct question 'What is the body-exposed-in-autumn-wind saying?' is also attested.
